findings.statement: The AI system the insurer uses for eligibility determination and premium calculation is a high-risk AI system: it is intended to be used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life insurance, a use case expressly listed in Annex III point 5(c), and all AI systems referred to in Annex III are high-risk under Article 6(2).

The system performs profiling of natural persons because it automatically processes applicants' personal data to evaluate personal aspects such as health and economic situation, so the Article 6(3) derogation from high-risk classification cannot apply: an Annex III system that performs profiling is always high-risk.

The insurer is a deployer of the system, since it uses the AI system under its own authority, and as a deployer of a high-risk AI system it must use the system in accordance with the instructions for use and must assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training, authority and support, which governs the employee reviewing the recommended premium.

The insurer must, to the extent it exercises control over the applicant data fed into the system, ensure that input data is relevant and sufficiently representative for the system's intended purpose, and must keep the logs automatically generated by the system under its control for at least six months unless Union or national data protection law provides otherwise.
Because the system makes or assists in making decisions concerning the applicants, the insurer must inform the applicants that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system.

The insurer must perform a fundamental rights impact assessment of the system prior to deploying it, as Article 27(1) expressly covers deployers of Annex III point 5(c) systems, and must afterwards notify the market surveillance authority of the results.

The applicants' medical information is data concerning health under Article 4(15), so its processing is prohibited under Article 9(1) unless a condition in Article 9(2) applies; the insurer may therefore process it for eligibility and premium setting only where such a condition is met.

The processing of applicants' personal data for eligibility and premium setting requires a lawful basis under Article 6(1); the scenario identifies none, so the processing is lawful only if and to the extent at least one basis in Article 6(1) covers it.

Whether the underwriting decision is one the applicants have a right not to be subject to under Article 22(1) turns on the employee review: the premium is recommended automatically but the policy is issued only after the review, so the decision is based solely on automated processing only if the employee's review does not meaningfully alter the outcome.

Where Article 22(1) is engaged, the insurer must implement the Article 22(3) safeguards, at least human intervention on the controller's part, the ability to express a point of view and to contest the decision, and because the decision rests on health data, Article 22(4) additionally requires that an Article 9(2)(a) or (g) condition applies and suitable safeguards are in place.

Where Article 22(1) or (4) is engaged, the insurer must, at the time the data are collected, inform applicants of the existence of the automated decision-making, including profiling, and give meaningful information about the logic involved and the significance and envisaged consequences of the processing.

The underwriting processing requires a data protection impact assessment prior to the processing: it is a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing, including profiling, on which decisions producing legal effects for the applicants are based, and as a deployer of a high-risk AI system the insurer must use the provider's Article 13 information to comply with this DPIA obligation.

The insurer is among the entities to which DORA applies: Article 2(1) lists insurance and reinsurance undertakings, which Article 2(2) collectively designates financial entities, subject to the exclusions in Article 2(3), one of which refers to insurance and reinsurance undertakings by cross-reference to Directive 2009/138/EC.

The AI system is an ICT asset of the insurer as software in the network and information systems it uses, so the insurer must identify, classify and document the AI-supported underwriting function and its supporting asset as part of the sound ICT risk management framework required by Article 6(1), reviewing the classification at least yearly.

The insurer's management body must define, approve, oversee and be responsible for the implementation of the ICT risk management arrangements under Article 6(1), including those covering the AI system.

summaries.relevance: Converts the insurer's pricing use case into high-risk status, which is the classification every deployer-duty and transparency conclusion in the answer depends on.
Names the insurer's exact use case, risk assessment and pricing of natural persons in life insurance, so the classification finding rests on an express list entry rather than analogy.
Defines the only escape route from the Annex III classification, and its profiling carve-out is what forecloses it for this system.
Supplies the role definition that attaches the deployer obligations to the insurer, which merely uses the system under its own authority.
Sets the baseline for how the insurer may operate the system inside its underwriting process.
Gives the scenario's employee review its regulatory content: oversight must be exercised by competent, trained personnel with authority and support.
Ties the insurer to the quality of the applicant data it feeds the system, which is where the medical information enters the AI Act framework.
Adds the log-retention floor the insurer must honour for the system, deferring to data protection law where it provides otherwise.
Creates the AI Act layer of applicant-facing information because the system makes or assists in decisions on natural persons.
Links the deployer's AI Act position to the GDPR impact assessment by directing high-risk deployers to use the provider's information for their DPIA compliance.
Imposes the fundamental rights impact assessment on this deployer by expressly listing Annex III point 5(c) systems, a deployment-precondition duty in its own right.
Completes the impact assessment process with the notification of its results to the market surveillance authority.
Supplies the profiling concept on which both the Article 22 analysis and the AI Act's profiling carve-out turn, covering automated evaluation of aspects such as health and economic situation.
Places the applicants' medical information inside the special-category regime the whole GDPR half of the answer is built on.
Carries the general lawfulness requirement that applies to all the eligibility and premium processing on top of the special-category question.
Makes the medical-information processing presumptively prohibited, setting the baseline the insurer's underwriting must be justified against.
Holds the only routes around the Article 9(1) prohibition and, through points (a) and (g), also feeds the Article 22(4) analysis.
Marks the boundary of the solely-automated decision regime, which is the pivotal issue the scenario's human-review detail raises.
Specifies the safeguard package the insurer owes applicants if the automated-decision route applies.
Couples the Article 22 regime to the special-category conditions, so health-based automated decisions need both an Article 9(2)(a) or (g) condition and safeguards.
Fixes the content of collection-stage transparency where automated decision-making under Article 22(1) and (4) is at stake.
Carries the prior impact-assessment duty that the specific triggers activate for this underwriting processing.
Names the insurer's processing, a systematic, extensive, automated evaluation of personal aspects with legal-effect decisions, as a mandatory DPIA trigger.
Lists insurance and reinsurance undertakings among the entities in scope, the entry point for the DORA half of the answer.
Collects the listed entities under the financial entity label that carries DORA's operative duties.
Contains the scope carve-outs that stand between the listing and a confirmed application of DORA to the insurer.
Classifies the AI pricing tool as an ICT asset, the definitional step that pulls it into the ICT risk regime.
Is the framework duty into which the AI system's risks and documentation must be integrated once scope is settled.
Sets the identification and documentation work for the AI-supported underwriting function, including its yearly review.
Fixes internal accountability by placing the framework's definition and approval on the management body.

actions: Settle the insurer's role on the AI value chain: who developed the system, whether it was placed on the market or put into service under another entity's name, and whether the insurer substantially modified it, since these facts determine whether the insurer also carries provider obligations under the AI Act.

Establish the Article 6(1) lawful basis and the Article 9(2) condition relied on for processing the applicants' medical information, and verify whether the insurer's Member State has introduced further conditions or limitations under Article 9(4).

Assess whether the employee review before issuance is meaningful enough that the decision is not based solely on automated processing within Article 22(1), and if it is engaged, determine which Article 22(2) gateway applies and confirm the Article 22(3) and 22(4) safeguards.

Verify against DORA Article 2(3) whether the insurer falls within any exclusion, one carve-out referring to insurance and reinsurance undertakings by cross-reference to Directive 2009/138/EC, whose scope cannot be resolved from the provided corpus.
Settle whether the AI system is operated in-house or by an ICT third-party service provider, since third-party operation would engage DORA's ICT third-party risk regime.
